cognate: Greek Zeus and Vedic dyaus continue *dyēws; patēr and pitṛ continue *ph₂tēr. The claim concerns these nouns, not an inferred verbal root for father.
drift_or_renewal: The Greek sky-name is a divine proper name; Vedic retains the transparent sky designation. Father remains the same inherited relational title.
shared_syntax: Father is predicated of or in apposition to the nominative sky deity: Greek patēr Zeus, Vedic dyaur ... pitā. Word order differs; this is an inherited nominal divine designation, not a claim of identical meter or clause syntax.
context: Homer invokes the paternal deity as guarantor of right conduct in battle; the Atharvavedic verse identifies Sky as father and progenitor alongside mother Earth. Both identify the same inherited celestial figure as father. The specific matching divine name plus kinship title, reinforced by recurrent Rigvedic nominatives and the vocative dyaus pitar, is stronger than ordinary father/son vocabulary. Both anchors are partners in BS-a4824; the Norse pivot is not evidence for this equation.

near_miss.lead: Night and darkness: nott/myrkast or myrkri alongside noći/mraka.
near_miss.why_not: The night words are cognate and the darkness words are mapped together, but the relations differ: Norse temporal setting plus superlative darkness or a prepositional phrase, versus Serbian fullness of darkness and a lament. Corpus searches show ordinary Norse darkness-at-night narration (including Egils saga 76v:38 and 81r:7), not a distinctive inherited construction. The late Serbian witnesses and obvious natural association weaken inheritance.

near_miss.lead: Arrive at midnight: kemr ... miðja nátt / uenisti media nocte.
near_miss.why_not: All three lexical components have cognate counterparts, but coming at midnight is a freely compositional time expression. Norse accusative with um and Latin temporal ablative do not preserve distinctive syntax. Searches found midnight across ordinary narrative, translated religious material, and Greek descriptive prose, including Herodotus 4.181.4 and 8.9.1. No special ritual or poetic context secures inheritance.

The Norse characters sleep at night; the Homeric lines emphasize sleepless nights, while the byliny use an ordinary bedtime formula. Shared sleep/night vocabulary does not establish the same figure or a marked construction.

near_miss.lead: Sun and dawn/east: sól ... austri; sūrya/uṣas; ēō/ēelion.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse locative east is a time-of-arrival marker, not the coordinated pair of deities. The Greek pair bounds the world, while the Vedic passages concern cosmic generation or the destinations of a wandering mind. Searches in RV also show lover/follower and light comparisons involving these nouns. Cognate material is secure, but these anchors do not establish one shared construction and function; no Norse inheritance claim is warranted.

near_miss.lead: Steal upon a sleeping victim: stalst ... sovanda / svapantīṃ tsarati, with waking contrasted.
near_miss.why_not: This is the closest unclaimed verbal comparison: both refer to covert approach to a sleeping victim, and both contrast waking in the immediate context. Sleep is securely cognate. The stela/tsar equation rests here on the external kaikki:tsel label, absent from the lexicon entries inspected; no qualified comparative derivation is supplied. Searches return only these two sleep-plus-tsel hits, and another Vedic tsar occurrence describes a bird approaching food. The hostile contexts are a human killing accusation versus a protective charm. Retain for etymological review rather than assert a securely inherited verbal formula.

near_miss.lead: Red gold: rautt gvll / красна золота.
near_miss.why_not: Gold is cognate but the color epithet is lexically renewed. Both are ornament contexts, yet this is a natural material description and the Russian witness is late; its shirt context is also textually awkward. The shared description alone does not distinguish inheritance from ordinary or renewed diction.

The Irish partner concerns appearance without clear understanding and a bellows comparison; it has no corresponding heart-burning collocation. Wider searches do find Vedic burning-heart images, recorded separately as a search lead, but no two slab anchors sustain that equation. Germanic searches also found translated Christian heart-burning language, so the image is not by itself evidence of prehistoric inheritance.

The Norse sword is the subject of biting in the immediate continuation, but the Sanskrit partner describes slaying enemies with anger and with a thunderbolt. It supplies no matching biting weapon phrase. The shared combat topic is insufficient.

The Norse sword ornament appears to move; the Homeric sword-belt bears a coiled, three-headed serpent. This is an interesting material-culture motif across slab passages, but Norse ormr and Greek drakōn are not cognate here and the verbs/attributes do not constitute shared wording. No inherited phrase is claimed.

search_lead.cognate: Norse hiarta (normalized hjarta, nominative singular) and Vedic hṛdayam/hṛtsu/hṛdaḥ continue the heart word *ḱerd-. The burning/heating verbs differ; no cognacy is asserted for them.
search_lead.argument: The Norse speaker describes his own heart burning and glowing in frustrated eagerness for combat, with a gold-glow comparison. RV 10.34 has cold dice burn the heart, an explicit emotional fire metaphor; RV 10.103 and AVP 12.21 turn heart-burning/heating against enemies. This provides possible semantic renewal around a cognate heart noun, but the emotional agents and transitivity differ, and fire-as-emotion can develop independently. Same-root Germanic search results include biblical heart-burning translations, a further reason not to presume antiquity. The Irish slab partner lacks the collocation, hence a search lead only.

error.correct_reading: Accusative singular of the mountain name Ossa; treat as a proper name and remove the speech-root mapping.
error.evidence: Coordinated with Olympus as one of the Thessalian mountains, followed by the valley between them; it is not the common noun for voice.

error.correct_reading: The segment belongs to mithunatvam, an abstract noun in -tva, accusative singular; not a possessive adjective meaning your.
error.evidence: The interrogative asks who knows the paired nature of Virāj. The displayed split mithuna tvam must not be analyzed as an independent pronoun or possessive.

error.correct_reading: Feminine singular tavna, from tavan (poetic/regional variant of taman, dark), agreeing with vocative noći.
error.evidence: The direct address to night and the following darkness noun make the adjective transparent. The unknown lemma is recoverable; no additional PIE assignment is proposed.
